course.title: C++ Beginner Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive 30-part beginner course taking you from absolute zero to confident C++ programmer. Covers fundamentals, memory management, OOP, STL, and real-world projects. C++ is the backbone of game engines, operating systems, browsers, embedded systems, and high-performance software.

blocks.value: Welcome to the World of C++

C++ is one of the most powerful and widely-used programming languages in the world. Created by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1985 as an extension of the C language, C++ adds object-oriented features while keeping C's low-level hardware control. It is a compiled language — meaning your code is translated into machine code before running, giving it unmatched performance.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing C++ code → compiler → machine code → CPU execution
blocks.caption: C++ is compiled directly to machine code for maximum performance

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Infographic/Diagram — A visual flowchart showing: 'Human writes C++ code' → 'Compiler (GCC/Clang/MSVC)' → 'Machine Code (.exe/.out)' → 'CPU executes directly'. Use arrows and icons. Highlight the compiler step as the key difference from interpreted languages. Use C++ blue (#00599C) and white colors.
Where is C++ Used?

C++ powers some of the most critical software on Earth:
• **Game Engines** — Unreal Engine, Unity (core), Godot, most AAA games
• **Operating Systems** — Windows, macOS, Linux kernels, Android
• **Browsers** — Chrome, Firefox, Safari rendering engines
• **Databases** — MySQL, MongoDB, Redis
• **Embedded Systems** — Cars, medical devices, IoT, spacecraft (NASA uses C++)
• **High-Frequency Trading** — Wall Street trading platforms
• **Graphics & Simulation** — Adobe Photoshop, Blender, AutoCAD
• **Compilers** — GCC, Clang, LLVM are written in C++

blocks.alt: C++ logo surrounded by icons representing games, OS, browsers, databases, cars, and finance
blocks.caption: C++ powers everything from video games to spacecraft

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Illustration — C++ logo (blue hexagon with '++') in the center with orbiting icons: game controller (games), OS window (operating systems), browser icon (Chrome/Firefox), database cylinder (MySQL), car (embedded/ADAS), rocket (space), stock chart (finance). Use official C++ blue (#00599C) and accent colors.
How C++ Differs from Other Languages

**C++ vs Python:** C++ is compiled (fast, direct CPU execution) while Python is interpreted (slower, runs via interpreter). C++ gives you manual memory control; Python handles memory automatically. C++ code is verbose but blazing fast; Python is concise but slower.

**C++ vs Java:** Both are compiled, but Java runs on a Virtual Machine (JVM) while C++ compiles directly to machine code. C++ offers pointers and manual memory management; Java uses garbage collection. C++ is closer to the hardware.

**C++ vs JavaScript:** JavaScript runs in browsers and is interpreted. C++ is a systems language with static typing and compilation. They serve completely different purposes.

**C++ vs C:** C++ is a superset of C — it includes everything C has, plus classes, objects, templates, exceptions, and the Standard Template Library (STL).
Your First C++ Program

Every C++ program needs a `main()` function — this is where execution begins. We use `cout` (character output) to print text, and `return 0` tells the operating system the program finished successfully.

blocks.question: What makes C++ different from Python in terms of execution?
options: C++ is interpreted, Python is compiled
C++ is compiled to machine code, Python is interpreted
Both are compiled to machine code
blocks.correctAnswer: C++ is compiled to machine code, Python is interpreted
blocks.explanation: C++ code is compiled directly into machine code that the CPU executes. Python code is read and executed line-by-line by an interpreter, which is slower.

blocks.question: Which of the following is NOT typically built with C++?
blocks.explanation: Simple static websites are typically built with HTML/CSS/JavaScript. C++ is used for performance-critical applications like game engines, OS kernels, and trading platforms.

blocks.question: What is the entry point (starting function) of every C++ program?
blocks.explanation: Every C++ program must have a main() function. Execution always starts from main().

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Setting Up Your C++ Environment

blocks.value: Installing Your C++ Toolkit

To write and run C++ code, you need two things: a **compiler** (translates C++ to machine code) and a **code editor** (where you write code). Unlike Python, C++ requires compilation before you can run your program.

blocks.alt: VS Code editor with C++ extension and terminal showing compilation command
blocks.caption: VS Code with C++ extension is the recommended editor for beginners

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — VS Code window showing the Extensions sidebar with 'C/C++' by Microsoft installed, and a hello.cpp file open in the editor with syntax highlighting. Terminal panel at bottom showing 'g++ hello.cpp -o hello'. Dark theme preferred.
Installing a Compiler

**Windows:** Install MinGW-w64 or use Visual Studio Community (includes MSVC compiler).
**macOS:** Install Xcode Command Line Tools by running `xcode-select --install` in Terminal.
**Linux:** Install GCC with `sudo apt install g++` (Ubuntu/Debian) or `sudo dnf install gcc-c++` (Fedora).

blocks.alt: Terminal windows on Windows, Mac, and Linux showing compiler version check commands
blocks.caption: Verify your compiler installation by checking its version

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — Three terminal windows side by side. Left: Windows Command Prompt showing 'g++ --version'. Middle: macOS Terminal showing 'clang++ --version'. Right: Linux Terminal showing 'g++ --version'. Each shows version output. Dark terminal themes.
The Compilation Process

C++ is a compiled language. You cannot run `.cpp` files directly. You must compile them first:
1. Write code in a `.cpp` file
2. Run the compiler: `g++ filename.cpp -o outputname`
3. Run the executable: `./outputname` (Linux/Mac) or `outputname.exe` (Windows)

**Compile:** `g++ hello.cpp -o hello`
**Run (Linux/Mac):** `./hello`
**Run (Windows):** `hello.exe`
Understanding #include and std::

`#include <iostream>` tells the compiler to include the input/output stream library. Without it, `std::cout` would not exist.

`std::` is the namespace for the C++ Standard Library. It prevents naming conflicts. You can also write `using namespace std;` to avoid typing `std::` repeatedly, but it's better practice to use the prefix in real projects.

blocks.question: What file extension is used for C++ source files?
blocks.explanation: .cpp is the most common and recommended extension for C++ source files. .c is for C, .cxx and .cc are also valid but less common.

blocks.question: Which command compiles a C++ file named program.cpp on Linux?
blocks.explanation: g++ is the GNU C++ compiler. The -o flag specifies the output executable name. You must compile before running.

blocks.question: What does std::cout do in C++?
blocks.explanation: std::cout (character output) is used to print text and values to the console/terminal. It's part of the iostream library.

blocks.value: Storing Data with Variables

In C++, you must declare a variable's type before using it. This is called **static typing** — the compiler needs to know how much memory to allocate. Unlike Python, you cannot change a variable's type after declaration.

blocks.alt: Memory diagram showing different variable types occupying different byte sizes in RAM
blocks.caption: Each data type occupies a specific amount of memory in RAM

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A horizontal RAM/memory strip divided into blocks of different sizes. int (4 bytes), float (4 bytes), double (8 bytes), char (1 byte), bool (1 byte). Each block labeled with type name and size. Use a technical but clean style with byte counts clearly visible.
Fundamental Data Types

**int** — Whole numbers (e.g., 42, -7, 0). Typically 4 bytes. Range: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647.
**float** — Single-precision decimals (e.g., 3.14f). 4 bytes. ~7 decimal digits of precision.
**double** — Double-precision decimals (e.g., 3.14159). 8 bytes. ~15 decimal digits of precision.
**char** — Single character (e.g., 'A', '$'). 1 byte. Must use single quotes.
**bool** — True or false. 1 byte. Values: true or false (lowercase).
**string** — Text (e.g., "Hello"). Requires `#include <string>`. Variable length.

blocks.output:
Name: Alice
Age: 25
Price: 19.99
PI: 3.14159
Grade: A
Active: 1

blocks.value: Variable Naming Rules

• Names can contain letters, numbers, and underscores
• Must start with a letter or underscore (NOT a number)
• Case-sensitive: `Score` and `score` are different
• Use **camelCase** or **snake_case**: `userName` or `user_name`
• Avoid C++ reserved words: int, class, return, if, while, etc.
• Cannot use special characters: @, #, $, %, -, etc.
sizeof() — Checking Memory Usage

C++ gives you control over memory. The `sizeof()` operator tells you exactly how many bytes a type or variable uses. This is crucial for understanding memory constraints, especially in embedded systems.

blocks.output:
Size of int: 4 bytes
Size of float: 4 bytes
Size of double: 8 bytes
Size of char: 1 bytes
Size of bool: 1 bytes

blocks.question: Which of the following is a valid C++ variable declaration?
blocks.explanation: C++ requires the type before the name, and names cannot start with numbers or contain hyphens. 'class' is also a reserved keyword.

blocks.question: What is the typical size of an int in C++?
blocks.explanation: On most modern systems, an int occupies 4 bytes (32 bits), giving it a range of approximately -2 billion to +2 billion.

blocks.question: Which operator checks how many bytes a variable or type uses?
blocks.explanation: sizeof(variable) or sizeof(type) returns the number of bytes the variable or type occupies in memory.

blocks.value: Constants and Type Modifiers

Sometimes you want values that never change — these are called **constants**. C++ also provides **type modifiers** that change the behavior and range of basic types, giving you fine-grained control over memory and data representation.
The const Keyword
Use `const` to declare a variable whose value cannot be modified after initialization. This prevents accidental changes and makes your intent clear to other programmers.
Type Modifiers: signed, unsigned, short, long

**signed** — Can hold positive and negative values (default for int).
**unsigned** — Can only hold positive values (0 and up), but doubles the positive range.
**short** — Reduces size (typically 2 bytes for short int).
**long** — Increases size (typically 4 or 8 bytes for long int).
**long long** — Even larger (typically 8 bytes).

blocks.alt: Number line showing signed int range (-2B to +2B) vs unsigned int range (0 to +4B)
blocks.caption: Unsigned types sacrifice negative range for double the positive range

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Two horizontal number lines. Top: signed int from -2,147,483,648 to +2,147,483,647. Bottom: unsigned int from 0 to 4,294,967,295. Use different colors. Show that unsigned has no negative side but extends further on the positive side.

blocks.output:
unsigned int: 4000000000
short int: 32000
long int: 2000000000
long long: 9000000000000
Size of short: 2 bytes
Size of long long: 8 bytes

blocks.value: Auto Keyword (C++11+)
Modern C++ lets the compiler infer the type with `auto`. This is convenient but use it carefully — explicit types make code more readable for beginners.

blocks.question: What happens if you try to modify a const variable after initialization?
blocks.explanation: const variables are read-only. The compiler will reject any attempt to modify them after initialization.

blocks.question: What is the main advantage of using unsigned int over signed int?
blocks.explanation: Unsigned types use the bit that would represent the sign to store more positive values, effectively doubling the maximum positive value.

blocks.question: Which keyword makes a variable unchangeable after initialization?
blocks.explanation: The const keyword creates a constant variable whose value cannot be modified after it is set.

blocks.value: Arithmetic, Comparison & Logical Operators

Operators are symbols that perform operations on values. C++ has the same three essential categories as most languages: arithmetic (math), comparison (checking equality), and logical (combining conditions). C++ also has unique operators for memory manipulation.

blocks.alt: Cheat sheet showing arithmetic, comparison, logical, and bitwise operators with examples
blocks.caption: Your quick reference guide to C++ essential operators

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Cheat Sheet/Infographic — A clean table divided into sections: Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), Comparison (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=), Logical (&&, ||, !), and Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>). Each operator shows symbol, name, and a mini example. Use monospace font for code examples. C++ blue theme.
Arithmetic Operators

`+` Addition, `-` Subtraction, `*` Multiplication, `/` Division (integer division truncates), `%` Modulus (remainder).

**Important:** When dividing two integers, C++ performs integer division (truncates the decimal). To get a decimal result, at least one operand must be a float or double.

blocks.output:
Addition: 22
Subtraction: 12
Multiplication: 85
Division (int): 3
Division (float): 3.4
Modulus: 2

blocks.value: Comparison Operators

These return `true` (1) or `false` (0):
`==` Equal to, `!=` Not equal to, `>` Greater than, `<` Less than, `>=` Greater than or equal, `<=` Less than or equal
Logical Operators

`&&` — AND: True if BOTH conditions are true
`||` — OR: True if AT LEAST ONE condition is true
`!` — NOT: Reverses the boolean value
Increment and Decrement Operators

C++ has special operators for adding or subtracting 1:
`++x` (pre-increment): increment first, then use
`x++` (post-increment): use first, then increment
`--x` and `x--` work the same way for subtraction.

blocks.question: What is the result of 17 / 5 when both are integers in C++?
blocks.explanation: C++ performs integer division when both operands are integers, truncating (cutting off) the decimal part. 17 / 5 = 3.4 becomes 3.

blocks.question: What does 10 % 3 return in C++?
blocks.explanation: % (modulus) gives the remainder after division. 10 divided by 3 is 3 with a remainder of 1.

blocks.question: Which operator increments a variable by 1?
blocks.explanation: The ++ operator increments a variable by 1. It can be used as prefix (++x) or postfix (x++).

parts.partTitle: Part 6: Input and Output (cin, cout, cerr)

blocks.value: Reading and Writing Data

C++ provides three standard streams for input and output: `cout` for normal output, `cin` for input, and `cerr` for error messages. These are part of the `<iostream>` library and are objects connected to your terminal.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing cin reading from keyboard into variables and cout writing to screen
blocks.caption: cin reads from keyboard, cout writes to screen, cerr writes errors

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Three labeled arrows. Arrow 1: Keyboard → cin → Variables. Arrow 2: Variables → cout → Screen. Arrow 3: Error data → cerr → Screen (in red). Use a clean flowchart style with distinct colors for each stream.
Reading Input with cin

`cin` (character input) reads data from the keyboard. The `>>` extraction operator pulls data from the input stream into a variable. `cin` automatically skips whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) between inputs.

blocks.output:
Enter your name: Alice
Enter your age: 25
Hello, Alice! You are 25 years old.

blocks.value: Reading Strings with Spaces: getline()

`cin >>` stops reading at the first whitespace. To read an entire line including spaces, use `getline()`. Be careful: if you mix `cin >>` and `getline()`, leftover newline characters can cause issues. Use `cin.ignore()` to clear the buffer.

blocks.output:
Enter your age: 25
Enter your full name: Alice Johnson
Name: Alice Johnson, Age: 25

blocks.value: cerr — The Error Stream

`cerr` works like `cout` but is dedicated to error messages. In production systems, `cerr` output can be redirected to log files while `cout` goes to the normal display. This separation is crucial for debugging and monitoring.

blocks.output:
Attempting division...
Error: Cannot divide by zero!

blocks.value: Formatting Output with setw and setprecision

The `<iomanip>` library provides tools to format output: `setw(n)` sets the width of the next output field, `setprecision(n)` controls decimal places for floating-point numbers, and `fixed` forces decimal notation.

blocks.question: Which function reads an entire line including spaces from the user?
blocks.explanation: getline() reads an entire line including spaces until it hits a newline. cin >> stops at the first whitespace.

blocks.question: Why should you use cin.ignore() before getline() after using cin >>?
options: To clear the leftover newline character from the buffer
blocks.correctAnswer: To clear the leftover newline character from the buffer
blocks.explanation: cin >> leaves a newline in the buffer. getline() sees this newline and thinks the user pressed Enter immediately. cin.ignore() removes it.

blocks.question: Which stream is used specifically for error messages in C++?
blocks.explanation: cerr (character error) is the standard error stream. Unlike cout, it is unbuffered and typically used for error and diagnostic messages.

blocks.value: Converting Between Types

C++ is a statically typed language, so you often need to convert values from one type to another. This is called **type casting** or **type conversion**. C++ offers multiple ways to cast, each with different safety guarantees.

blocks.alt: Flowchart showing implicit vs explicit casting paths between int, float, double, and char
blocks.caption: C++ supports both automatic (implicit) and manual (explicit) type conversions

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Two paths side by side. Left: 'Implicit Casting' showing int → float automatically with a green arrow. Right: 'Explicit Casting' showing (int)3.7 with a blue arrow to 3. Include warning signs for dangerous casts like float to int (data loss).
Implicit Conversion (Automatic)
C++ automatically converts smaller types to larger types to prevent data loss. This happens when you assign a smaller type to a larger type variable, or mix types in expressions.

blocks.output:
Result: 7.5
Type of result: double
ASCII of 'A': 65

blocks.value: Explicit Casting (C-Style)
Use `(type)value` or `type(value)` to force a conversion. Be careful — explicit casts can cause data loss when converting from larger to smaller types (e.g., double to int truncates the decimal).
Modern C++ Casts (static_cast, etc.)

Modern C++ provides safer casting operators: `static_cast<type>(value)` for standard conversions, `dynamic_cast` for polymorphic types, `const_cast` for removing const, and `reinterpret_cast` for low-level bit reinterpretation. As a beginner, focus on `static_cast`.

blocks.output:
Original: 42.7
static_cast to int: 42
Char from 66: B

blocks.value: Narrowing Conversions and Data Loss

When casting from a larger type to a smaller type, data can be lost. C++11 introduced **list initialization** with `{}` which prevents narrowing conversions — the compiler will throw an error if data loss would occur.

blocks.question: What is the result of static_cast<int>(5.9)?
blocks.explanation: Casting a double to int truncates (cuts off) the decimal part. It does NOT round. static_cast<int>(5.9) gives 5.

blocks.question: Which C++11 initialization syntax prevents narrowing conversions?
blocks.explanation: Brace initialization {} prevents narrowing. int x{5.5} would cause a compile error because 5.5 cannot fit in an int without data loss.

blocks.question: Which modern C++ cast operator is recommended for standard type conversions?
blocks.explanation: static_cast<type>(value) is the recommended way for explicit conversions in modern C++. It is safer and more explicit than C-style casts.

blocks.value: Making Decisions in Code

Programs need to make decisions. Conditional statements let your code execute different blocks based on whether a condition is true or false. In C++, conditions use curly braces `{}` to define blocks — unlike Python which uses indentation.

blocks.alt: Decision tree diagram showing if, else if, else branches with conditions and outcomes
blocks.caption: Conditional statements create branches in your program's execution flow

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Flowchart — A top-down diamond-shaped flowchart: Start → Diamond 'score >= 90?' → Yes branch → 'Grade A' → End. No branch → Diamond 'score >= 80?' → Yes → 'Grade B' → End. No → Diamond 'score >= 70?' → Yes → 'Grade C' → End. No → 'Grade F' → End. Use different colors for each grade path.
The if Statement
The `if` statement executes a block of code only if its condition evaluates to true. The condition goes inside parentheses `()`, and the block goes inside curly braces `{}`.
if-else and else-if
Use `else` to run code when the if condition is false. Use `else if` to check additional conditions. C++ checks conditions from top to bottom and stops at the first true condition.
Nested if Statements
You can place if statements inside other if statements. This is called nesting. Be careful with too many levels — it makes code harder to read. Each nested block needs its own set of curly braces.
The Ternary Operator

For simple if-else assignments, C++ offers the ternary operator: `condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false`. It is a compact one-liner but should only be used for simple cases to keep code readable.

blocks.question: What brackets define a code block in C++ conditionals?
blocks.explanation: C++ uses curly braces {} to define code blocks. Unlike Python, indentation is for readability only and does not affect block structure.

blocks.question: What does this ternary expression return? int x = (5 > 10) ? 100 : 200;
blocks.explanation: 5 > 10 is false, so the ternary operator returns the value after the colon, which is 200.

blocks.question: Which keyword marks the block that runs when all previous if conditions are false?
blocks.explanation: The else block runs only when none of the preceding if or else if conditions were true.

blocks.value: Switch: A Cleaner Alternative to Many if-else

When you need to compare a single variable against many constant values, `switch` is cleaner and often faster than a chain of if-else statements. The switch statement compares an expression against case labels and jumps directly to the matching one.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing switch statement jumping directly to matching case label
blocks.caption: Switch jumps directly to the matching case — often faster than multiple if-else checks

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A box labeled 'switch(day)' with arrows jumping directly to case labels: case 1 → Monday, case 2 → Tuesday, etc. Show a 'default' arrow for unmatched values. Use a clean routing/jump visual with distinct colors per case.
Basic Switch Syntax
The `switch` statement evaluates an expression and matches it against `case` labels. Each case ends with `break` to prevent fall-through to the next case. The `default` case handles unmatched values.
Fall-Through Behavior

Without `break`, execution falls through to the next case. This is sometimes intentional (like cases 6 and 7 sharing the same code above), but usually it's a bug. Always include `break` unless fall-through is deliberate.
Switch Limitations

Switch has important restrictions:
• The expression must be an integer, char, or enum (NOT float, double, or string)
• Case values must be constant expressions (not variables)
• You cannot use ranges like `case > 5:`
• For strings or ranges, use if-else instead

blocks.question: What happens if you forget break in a switch case?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
blocks.correctAnswer: Execution falls through to the next case
blocks.explanation: Without break, execution continues into the next case. This is called fall-through and is usually a bug unless intentionally used.

blocks.question: Which of these CANNOT be used as a switch expression in C++?
blocks.explanation: Switch expressions must be integral types (int, char, enum). Floating-point types like float and double are not allowed because exact equality comparisons are unreliable with floats.

blocks.question: Which keyword handles values that don't match any case in a switch?
blocks.explanation: The default case runs when no other case matches. It is optional but recommended for handling unexpected values.

blocks.value: Iterating with For Loops

A for loop lets you repeat a block of code a specific number of times. The C++ for loop has three parts: initialization, condition, and update — all separated by semicolons and enclosed in parentheses.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing for loop structure: init, condition, update, and body with arrows
blocks.caption: The three parts of a C++ for loop: initialization, condition, and update

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A circular flowchart showing for loop anatomy: Box 'int i = 0' (init) → Diamond 'i < 5?' (condition) → Yes → Box 'cout << i' (body) → Box 'i++' (update) → back to diamond. No → End. Label each part clearly with arrows.
Basic For Loop
The for loop syntax is: `for (initialization; condition; update) { body }`. The initialization runs once, the condition is checked before each iteration, and the update runs after each iteration.
For Loop Variations

You can customize the initialization, condition, and update. Count backwards, use different increments, or start from any value. You can also declare the loop variable outside the for statement (older C++ style).
break and continue
`break` exits the loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one. These work the same way in for loops as they do in while loops.
Range-Based For Loop (C++11)
Modern C++ introduces the range-based for loop, which iterates over collections without managing an index. It is cleaner and less error-prone than traditional for loops when you don't need the index.

blocks.question: How many times does this loop run? for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
blocks.explanation: The loop runs while i < 5, so i takes values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — that's 5 iterations. When i becomes 5, the condition is false and the loop stops.

blocks.question: What does continue do inside a for loop?
blocks.explanation: continue stops the current iteration early and jumps to the update expression, then checks the condition for the next iteration.

blocks.question: Which C++11 loop syntax iterates over a collection without an index variable?
blocks.explanation: The range-based for loop (for (auto item : collection)) iterates over each element directly without managing an index counter.

blocks.value: Repeating with Conditions

While loops repeat a block of code as long as a condition remains true. Use them when you don't know in advance how many times to loop — for example, waiting for user input or processing data until a condition is met.

blocks.alt: Flowchart showing while loop: check condition, execute block, repeat until false
blocks.caption: A while loop checks the condition BEFORE each iteration

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Flowchart — Circular flowchart: Diamond 'count > 0?' → Yes → Box 'cout << count' → Box 'count--' → back to diamond. No → 'End'. Show counter changing from 3 → 2 → 1 → 0. Use a clean loop arrow style.
While Loop
The while loop checks the condition before each iteration. If the condition is false from the start, the loop body never executes.
Do-While Loop
The do-while loop checks the condition AFTER each iteration. This guarantees the body runs at least once. Use it when you need to execute code before checking the condition — like menu systems.

blocks.output:
Enter a positive number: -5
That's not positive. Try again.
Enter a positive number: 0
That's not positive. Try again.
Enter a positive number: 7
You entered: 7

blocks.value: Infinite Loops and How to Avoid Them
If your condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever. Always ensure something inside the loop changes the condition variable. Use Ctrl+C to terminate an infinite loop in the terminal.

blocks.output:
1. Play
2. Settings
3. Quit
Choice: 1
You chose option 1

1. Play
2. Settings
3. Quit
Choice: 3
Goodbye!

blocks.value: While vs Do-While vs For

**Use for** when you know the exact number of iterations (e.g., counting 1 to 10).
**Use while** when you don't know the count but have a clear condition (e.g., reading until EOF).
**Use do-while** when the body must run at least once (e.g., input validation menus).

blocks.question: What is the key difference between while and do-while?
options: do-while checks condition after the body runs
while can only use int conditions
blocks.correctAnswer: do-while checks condition after the body runs
blocks.explanation: do-while guarantees the body executes at least once because the condition is checked after each iteration, not before.

blocks.question: Which loop type is best for a menu that must display at least once?
blocks.explanation: do-while is perfect for menus because it always shows the menu at least once, then repeats based on user input.

blocks.question: Which operator decreases a variable by 1 in C++?
blocks.explanation: The -- operator decrements a variable by 1. It can be prefix (--x) or postfix (x--).

blocks.value: Your First Collection: Arrays

An array is a fixed-size collection of elements of the same type, stored in contiguous memory. Once declared, the size cannot change. Arrays are the foundation of all other collections in C++ and are essential for understanding memory layout.

blocks.alt: Memory diagram showing array elements stored contiguously in RAM with indices
blocks.caption: Array elements are stored side-by-side in contiguous memory locations

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A horizontal RAM strip showing 5 contiguous memory blocks. Each block labeled with index (0-4) and value. Show memory addresses increasing by 4 bytes (for int array). Use a technical memory visualization style with hex addresses.
Declaring and Initializing Arrays

Arrays are declared with the type, name, and size in square brackets. You can initialize them at declaration or assign values later. The size must be a constant expression — you cannot use a variable for the size in standard C++ arrays.
Accessing and Modifying Array Elements

Access elements using square brackets with the index (starting at 0). You can read and write to any valid index. Accessing an index outside the array bounds causes **undefined behavior** — the program may crash, corrupt memory, or appear to work. C++ does NOT check bounds automatically.

blocks.output:
First: 10
Last: 50
Modified third: 99
All elements: 10 20 99 40 50

blocks.value: Finding Array Size
Use `sizeof(array) / sizeof(array[0])` to calculate the number of elements. This only works with actual arrays (not pointers). Forgetting to calculate size correctly is a common source of bugs.

blocks.output:
Array size: 6
Total bytes: 24
Element size: 4
5 10 15 20 25 30

blocks.value: Multidimensional Arrays
C++ supports arrays with multiple dimensions. A 2D array is like a grid or table — rows and columns. You can have 3D, 4D, and higher, but they become complex to manage.

blocks.question: What is the index of the first element in a C++ array?
blocks.explanation: C++ uses zero-based indexing. The first element is always at index 0. This is the same as Python and most C-family languages.

blocks.question: What happens if you access an array index that is out of bounds?
options: Undefined behavior (may crash or corrupt memory)
blocks.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior (may crash or corrupt memory)
blocks.explanation: C++ does NOT perform bounds checking on arrays. Accessing out-of-bounds memory causes undefined behavior — the program might crash, read garbage data, or silently corrupt memory.

blocks.question: Which formula calculates the number of elements in a C++ array?
blocks.explanation: sizeof(array) gives total bytes, sizeof(array[0]) gives bytes per element. Dividing them gives the element count. This only works with actual arrays, not pointers.
